openers.proterozoic-eon: The Proterozoic is the eon in which Earth's air changed for good. Free oxygen built up in the air and shallow seas, turning a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change never reversed. It reshaped everything it touched: banded iron formations precipitated across most continents, new minerals multiplied, and the gas proved toxic to many of the anaerobic microbes that had ruled until then. Ice spread in the Huronian glaciations, and a supercontinent began to rift apart above plumes of magma.
openers.paleoproterozoic-era: The Paleoproterozoic opens with the planet rusting. Massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents as oxygen met the iron dissolved in seawater, and the Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity. Life paid a price, since free oxygen was toxic to a biosphere built of anaerobes. On land, rifting began to split a low-latitude supercontinent, giant swarms of dikes cut the cratons, and a series of glaciations left their boulder beds near Lake Huron.
openers.siderian-period: The Siderian takes its name from the Greek word for iron, and iron is its signature. Banded iron formations piled up across most continents, their red layers made of oxidized iron. At the same time oxygen began to build up in the air for the first time, an irreversible change that may have wiped out many early organisms. Plume-driven rifting cracked a supercontinent, the Mistassini dikes cut the Superior Craton, and the first of the Huronian ice ages began.
openers.rhyacian-period: The Rhyacian is the period of the first complex cells. Eukaryotes are thought to have arisen when an Asgard archaeon took in an alphaproteobacterium, and sexual reproduction probably appeared too. Oxygen surged, leaving the largest carbon isotope excursion known and the first continental red beds, while the Makganyene ice may have frozen the planet as far as the tropics. By the period's end, collisions in West Africa and South America had begun gathering Earth's continents into the supercontinent Columbia.
openers.orosirian-period: The Orosirian is a period of giant blows and great collisions. An asteroid perhaps 20–25 km wide struck South Africa's Kaapvaal craton, and nearby, magma rose to form the largest layered intrusion in Earth's crust. Around the world, mountain belts stitched cratons together: Baltica from three blocks, Laurentia through the Trans-Hudson orogeny, Atlantica from West African and South American cratons. Meanwhile, black chert on the shore of Lake Superior preserved microbes like cyanobacteria.

reviews.neoarchean-era: The Neoarchean finished the job of building continents. Cratons stabilized on deep roots, welded along belts like the Limpopo and the Superior's Algoman collisions, and may have gathered into Kenorland and Arctica. By the eon's end continental crust was about 40 km thick and had likely risen above the sea. Volcanism ran at full heat, from komatiite floods and the Blake River supervolcano to the Ventersdorp lavas and the Great Dyke. Life kept pace: stromatolite reefs spread, and as nickel dwindled and oxygen came in pulses, the stage was being set for a changed atmosphere.
reviews.siderian-period: The Siderian is the period when oxygen won. Cyanobacteria had been making it for ages, but only once surface iron, sulfur and methane were used up did it build up in the air, rusting the seas into banded iron formations and multiplying the planet's minerals. The new gas was toxic to anaerobic life, perhaps causing the first known mass extinction. By destroying methane, it also weakened the greenhouse and helped bring on the Huronian ice. Below, plumes and dike swarms began to tear a supercontinent apart.
reviews.rhyacian-period: The Rhyacian shows oxygen reshaping both rock and life. The huge Lomagundi-Jatuli carbon swing records a surge of oxygen and buried organic matter, red beds show iron rusting on land, and the Makganyene ice may have reached the tropics. Amid these changes, eukaryotes probably arose, though early claims, including Gabon's Francevillian disks, are disputed. On the move below, the Eburnean and Transamazonian collisions began assembling Columbia, while a Karelian lagoon stored the carbon that became shungite.

arch-068.title: The continents rise from the sea
arch-068.text: For most of the Archean, there was almost nowhere to stand. Much continental crust lay under a superocean deeper than today's, and Paleoarchean crust was still submerged. Only at the end of the eon did the continents likely rise above the water. By then the continental crust was essentially formed, about 40 km thick. As land emerged, more continental weathering brought the oxygen isotopes of the oceans down toward modern levels.

prot-003.title: Banded iron formations reach their peak
prot-003.text:
Most of the iron ore that built the modern world was laid down around 2.5 billion years ago. At that time, massive banded iron formations precipitated across most continents, and deposition peaked. Their red layers are oxidized iron; the Siderian period takes its name from the Greek for iron.

Deposition began on the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons. Australia's Brockman Supersequence, 2500–2449 million years old, holds iron-formation sediments laid down as seas rose. The Hamersley Range iron formations, laid down 2470–2450 million years ago, are the world's thickest and most extensive, over 900 m thick.

prot-002.title: Oxygen multiplies the world's minerals
prot-002.text: More than two-thirds of all mineral species owe their existence to life. The Great Oxygenation Event set off explosive growth in mineral diversity, as many elements near the surface took oxidized forms. About 2,500 new minerals formed in the oxygenation stage from 2.5 to 1.9 billion years ago, lifting the total above 4,000. Oxidized uraninite, a uranium ore, alone gave rise to over 200 new uranyl minerals.

prot-004.title: Kenorland breaks apart
prot-004.text:
A supercontinent took hundreds of millions of years to tear itself apart. Between 2.48 and 2.45 billion years ago, rifting driven by plumes of magma began in a supercontinent that had sat at low latitudes, usually identified as {{ref:arch-052}}. The drawn-out breakup left mafic dikes, rift basins and rifted margins on many continents through the Siderian and Rhyacian. Final breakup produced large swarms of mafic dikes and sills across the North American provinces 2.2–2.1 billion years ago.

Its fragments became proto-continents including Laurentia, Baltica, the Yilgarn craton and Kalahari, and the breakup is associated with the era's glaciations. Kenorland itself is hypothetical. In the alternative view, the Sclavia supercraton broke up during a global pulse of mantle-plume magma around 2.33–2.1 billion years ago.

prot-005.title: The Matachewan dike swarm
prot-005.text: Thousands of magma-filled cracks mark where a continent began to split. About 2470 million years ago the Mistassini dike swarm, itself a large igneous province over 100,000 km², cut the Superior Craton. A large igneous province is a vast outpouring of magma. The related Matachewan swarm followed, covering at least 300,000 km² between Lake Superior and James Bay. Both are read as rifting above a hotspot near Sudbury, Ontario, at the onset of {{ref:prot-004}}.

prot-006.title: The Great Oxidation Event
prot-006.text:
Once, there was no oxygen in the air to breathe. Then, early in the Proterozoic, free oxygen built up in the atmosphere and shallow seas for the first time. It turned a weakly reducing atmosphere into an oxidizing one, and the change was irreversible. Every breathing animal since depends on it.

Cyanobacteria, the first known oxygen producers, are generally credited. They had been releasing oxygen for a long time, as in {{ref:arch-034}}. But oxygen won out only once surface reductants, chemicals that grab oxygen such as ferrous iron, sulfur and methane, were used up.

The rise was steep. Between 2410 and 2320 million years ago, the oxygen partial pressure climbed from about two millionths of a bar to at least two thousandths. By the end of the event, oxygen had risen from almost none to as much as 10% of the modern level.

The rocks record the switch. Sulfur isotope anomalies typical of an oxygen-free sky vanish after 2.4–2.3 billion years ago, and rust-red beds appear in soils by 2.3 billion.

prot-007.title: The Oxygen Catastrophe, the first mass extinction
prot-007.text:
The gas that sustains animals today was, at first, a poison. Free oxygen was toxic to the mostly anaerobic biosphere, and it may have wiped out many early organisms, mostly colonies of archaea, an ancient group of single-celled microbes. It is described as the first known mass extinction, killing most of the planet's obligate anaerobes, organisms that cannot survive oxygen.

It may have been the worst ever, but early life is too poorly known to compare it with the Big Five extinctions of later times. It is also the only well-documented extinction before the Phanerozoic, since earlier life was microbial or soft-bodied and left few fossils.

prot-008.title: Turee Creek microfossils and reefs
prot-008.text: Black chert, a hard glassy silica rock, in Australia's Turee Creek Group preserves some of the oldest known microfossils, dated to 2450 million years. Some of these carbon-rich fossils have been interpreted as iron-oxidizing bacteria, microbes that lived by rusting iron. The group also holds the Kazput Reef Complex, dated 2400–2300 million years old, the oldest known reef complex of the Proterozoic.

prot-010.title: The Sleaford orogeny shapes the Gawler Craton
prot-010.text: South Australia's oldest crust was born crumpled. The Gawler craton formed about 2,440 million years ago, and the Sleaford orogeny deformed it from 2440 to 2420 million years ago. It did not settle down quickly. Before 1550 million years ago, the craton was a set of active mountain belts reaching back to at least 2450 million years.

prot-009.title: The Dhala impact in India
prot-009.text: India's largest impact scar is a puzzle in both size and age. An impact struck the Bundelkhand craton and left the largest impact structure in the country. Its diameter is estimated at 3 km by some sources and 11 km by others. Its age is poorly constrained, somewhere between about 2.44 and 2.24 billion years ago, so how it fits into Earth's story remains uncertain.

prot-011.title: Dike swarms cut Scotland and Australia
prot-011.text: Scotland and Western Australia share a moment of cracking. The Scourie dike swarm, a set of magma-filled cracks, cut Scotland's Lewisian gneisses, overlapping a phase of crustal deformation called the Inverian at the start of the Proterozoic. Around 2410 million years ago, the Widgiemooltha swarm intruded the Yilgarn Craton, close in time to the Sebanga Poort dike in Zimbabwe.

prot-012.title: The Ongeluk filaments, perhaps the first fungi
prot-012.text: Fungi-like life may have lived inside volcanic rock 2.4 billion years ago. Filaments that grew inside cracks and gas bubbles of basalt in South Africa's Ongeluk Formation have been suggested to be fossils of fungus-like organisms. They are the earliest fossils with features typical of fungi: bottom-dwelling, multicellular, with threads able to fuse together. Ukraine's much younger Volyn biota is cited as further support for their fungal nature.

prot-013.title: The Huronian glaciation
prot-013.text:
Oxygen, the gas of life, may have plunged the planet into its first great ice age. Rising oxygen cut atmospheric methane from 300 to 4 ppmv, parts per million by volume, weakening the greenhouse that had kept Earth warm. Average global temperatures fell below 0 °C.

The result was a series of glacial periods, also called the Makganyene glaciation. It is named for diamictite-bearing rocks of the Huronian Supergroup near Lake Huron; diamictite is a jumble of boulders and mud dropped by ice. The Siderian record dates three pulses: about 2440–2420 million years ago (Duitschland), 2380–2360 million (Makganyene) and 2340–2310 million (Gowganda or Rietfontein).

The ice was widespread. Glacial deposits occur on six cratons, including Wyoming, Kaapvaal and Karelia-Kola, and correlate with beds in Western Australia. This is the earliest well-established ice age, with ice on land. Only {{ref:arch-041}} is older.

prot-015.title: Makganyene, a possible snowball Earth
prot-015.text: Ice may have reached the equator 2.2 billion years ago. South Africa's Makganyene glaciation has been proposed as a snowball Earth, a near-total freeze of the planet, set off by the evolution of cyanobacteria. Its glacial sediments, slightly younger than the Huronian deposits, were possibly laid down at tropical latitudes. Paleomagnetic evidence, the magnetism frozen into rocks, places South African glacial deposits of 2.2 billion years near the equator. Cap carbonates, limestone layers typical of the end of a deep freeze, sit above its glacial beds.

prot-014.title: The Lomagundi-Jatuli carbon swing
prot-014.text:
Seafloor limestones from this time hold the strangest carbon signal in Earth's history. Marine carbonates record the largest and longest-lasting positive carbon isotope excursion known, with δ13C values of +5 to +30‰. Put simply, the carbon in the sea became unusually heavy, because life buries the light carbon it takes up.

Matching it would have needed the burial of organic carbon to double or triple for millions of years. It accompanied a massive rise in atmospheric oxygen, an expansion of life and more burial of organic matter. Oxygen climbed around 2.3 billion years ago, then fell around 2.1 billion in the Shunga-Francevillian event, letting organic-rich black shales accumulate. If the excursion was globally synchronous, it lasted between about 128 and 249 million years.

prot-016.title: The Yarrabubba impact
prot-016.text: An asteroid may have punched through a sheet of ice to hit Western Australia. The impactor, about 7 km wide, struck the Yilgarn craton and left a crater 30–70 km across. Its date, 2.229 billion years ago, falls near the end of the Huronian glaciation, and simulations fit an impact into a 2-km-thick ice sheet. It was the oldest impact structure of confident age until 2025, when Miralga displaced it, and a later study challenged its date, suggesting a much younger impact.

prot-017.title: The Eburnean orogeny shapes West Africa
prot-017.text:
West Africa's ancient heart was assembled in one long episode of mountain building. The Eburnean orogeny was a series of tectonic, metamorphic and plutonic events, the last meaning magma intruded and cooled underground. It built the Eglab and Man shields of the West African Craton and structured its Birimian domain.

Together with the Transamazonian orogeny, it welded South American and West African cratons, an early step toward Columbia. Around 2070 million years ago, an upwelling of the asthenosphere, the soft layer beneath the plates, released a large volume of magma after the mountains had formed.

prot-018.title: The first red beds rust on land
prot-018.text: Red rock is a sign of oxygen in the air. Continental red beds formed as iron in weathered sandstone was exposed to oxygen and rusted to hematite, a red iron oxide. The first were laid down in the Rhyacian, signaling rising atmospheric oxygen. Iron in ancient soils shows oxygen reaching 5–18% of present levels around 2,200 million years ago, a big step from the near-zero of the Archean.

prot-019.title: The first eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus
prot-019.text:
Every plant, animal and fungus descends from a single act of swallowing. Eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, are thought to have arisen in the Rhyacian when an Asgard archaeon, a single-celled microbe, took in an alphaproteobacterium. The swallowed bacterium stayed on inside its host. Sexual reproduction probably appeared then too.

The earliest known eukaryotic acritarchs, organic-walled microfossils, date from between 2150 and 1950 million years ago. Yet when eukaryotes first appeared is debated. Claimed eukaryote records from 2.1 billion years ago are considered questionable. Another view puts the earliest evidence at 1.85 billion years, from symbiogenesis, the merging of archaea and proteobacteria under the new stress of oxygen. The oldest unambiguous eukaryote remains, from China, are 1.8–1.6 billion years old. Whatever the exact date, the rise of oxygen in {{ref:prot-006}} probably set the scene.

prot-020.title: The Transamazonian orogeny
prot-020.text: Parts of Brazil and the Guianas were made when two small continents collided. The Gavião and Jequié blocks, Archean proto-continents, ran into each other in the Transamazonian orogeny. The collision shaped what are now the São Francisco Craton and the Guiana Shield. Together with West Africa's {{ref:prot-017}}, it marks the start of Columbia's assembly, the gathering of a new supercontinent.

prot-022.title: The Francevillian disks of Gabon
prot-022.text:
Strange disks up to 17 cm across lie flattened in Gabon's black shales. They come from the Francevillian B Formation, about 2.1 billion years old. Some authors read them as the earliest multicellular life and the earliest eukaryotes, and a 2023 isotope study found an enrichment in light zinc that could reflect eukaryotic metabolism.

Whether they are fossils at all is disputed. A 2017 review called their biological origin questionable. A 2023 review suggested they may be artifacts of diagenesis, the chemical changes that turn sediment into rock. Recent reviews lean toward a non-biological origin.

prot-021.title: Columbia, a supercontinent assembles
prot-021.text:
Almost every piece of continent on Earth was once gathered into one. Global-scale collisions gathered almost all continental blocks into the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna.

Its proto-cratons became the cores of Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, possibly with Siberia, North China and Kalaharia. The collisions that joined them have their own names: the Trans-Hudson, Limpopo, Capricorn and Trans-North China orogenies. Each was a long-running crash of crust that left a mountain belt behind.

The mountains were huge. Zircons record an extensive high range, the Nuna Supermountains, between 2.0 and 1.8 billion years ago. Eroding peaks of that scale would have fed sediment and nutrients to the seas.

Columbia may also mark a change in how the planet works. Modern plate tectonics may have emerged by at least 2.2 billion years ago, with Columbia's formation, linking back to the debate in {{ref:arch-039}}.

prot-023.title: Shungite, Earth's oldest petroleum
prot-023.text: Some of the oldest oil on Earth formed in a lagoon in Russian Karelia. Organic-rich muds settled there in brackish water during active rifting, and volcanic nutrients may have raised biological productivity. The sequence is dated by a 1980 ± 27 million-year-old gabbro intrusion and underlying dolomites of 2090 ± 70 million years. The deposit holds over 250 gigatonnes of carbon. Metamorphism turned these oil source rocks into shungite, and its veins are migrated petroleum, now bitumen, of confirmed biological origin.

prot-025.title: The Bushveld Igneous Complex
prot-025.text: Most of the world's platinum comes from one frozen magma body in South Africa. Mantle magma rose through long cracks in the Kaapvaal crust and formed the largest layered igneous intrusion in Earth's crust. Layered like a cake, it includes three platinum-bearing layers called reefs. It holds the world's largest reserves of platinum-group metals, plus vast amounts of iron, tin, chromium, titanium and vanadium. The intrusion predates the nearby {{ref:prot-026}} by about 30 million years.

prot-026.title: The Vredefort impact, Earth's largest crater
prot-026.text:
The largest verified impact structure on Earth lies just south of Johannesburg. About 2.02 billion years ago, an asteroid struck the Kaapvaal craton in today's South Africa. It was first put at 10–15 km wide; in 2022 it was estimated at 20–25 km.

The original crater was 170–300 km across, possibly larger than Chicxulub. Little of it survives as a hole. Erosion of 7–11 km has removed the crater itself. What remains is the Vredefort Dome, a 70 km ring of hills that is the crater's rebounded central uplift, where deep rock sprang back up after the blow.

It was one of two of the largest known impacts of the Orosirian. It also left a gift. By dropping the Witwatersrand rocks down, the strike preserved rich gold deposits, laid down in {{ref:arch-043}}, that would otherwise have been eroded away.

prot-028.title: The Glenburgh orogeny joins Pilbara and Yilgarn
prot-028.text: Western Australia's two great cratons were joined in a single collision. The Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane, a block of crust with its own history, collided with the Yilgarn craton in the Glenburgh orogeny. The crash brought substantial granite magmatism to the Glenburgh Terrane. It also brought intense deformation and metamorphism, the remaking of rock by heat and pressure. Two cratons that had evolved apart now formed one block.

prot-029.title: Atlantica, a continent spanning the future Atlantic
prot-029.text: Africa and South America were neighbors long before Pangaea. Around 2 billion years ago, cratons now in West Africa and eastern South America joined to form the continent Atlantica. It included Amazonia and the Congo, West Africa and North Africa cratons. It is not generally regarded as a supercontinent, since it gathered only part of the world's land.

prot-032.title: The Svecofennian orogeny builds Scandinavia
prot-032.text:
The bedrock of Sweden and Finland is the root of a mountain range that has long since vanished. The Svecofennian orogeny affected what are now Sweden, Finland and Russia, joining cratons of Baltica within Columbia. Subduction closed an ocean basin and, about 1950 million years ago, emplaced the Jormua and Outokumpu ophiolites, slices of ocean floor pushed onto land.

Continent–continent collision lasted from 1870 to 1790 million years ago, overlapping with extension in the south. Then the mountains collapsed under their own weight, from 1790 to 1770 million years ago.

prot-034.title: The Trans-Hudson orogeny forges North America
prot-034.text:
The core of North America was welded together along a single great seam. The Trans-Hudson orogeny is the largest Paleoproterozoic mountain belt in the world, and it formed the Canadian Shield and the North American craton, Laurentia. It sutured the Hearne-Rae, Superior and Wyoming cratons into the continent's core.

Old cratonic blocks, island arcs and ocean deposits were folded, thrust, metamorphosed and intruded by hundreds of huge granite bodies. Final closure of the Manikewan Ocean around 1.83 billion years ago merged the Hearne, Superior and Sask cratons, and metamorphism peaked about 1.82–1.8 billion years ago. Following the Wopmay orogeny, it was the culminating event of Laurentia's assembly from six or seven Archean fragments.

prot-030.title: Baltica assembles from three blocks
prot-030.text: The ancient core of Europe was built from three pieces. Baltica formed from the collision of Fennoscandia, Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia. Sarmatia and Volgo-Uralia joined first, as Proto-Baltica, around 2.0 billion years ago. Proto-Baltica then collided with Fennoscandia about 1.8–1.7 billion years ago. One account puts the meeting of Sarmatia and Fennoscandia at 1.84–1.82 billion years ago, after a calm period following subduction.
